newsitem.title: CHINA: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Philippines props up peso.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Philippines props up peso.

text.p: If evidence was needed that selling pressure on some Asian currencies has yet to disappear, the Philippines' central bank provided it on Monday.
The central bank raised its overnight borrowing rate to 26 percent from 22 percent to protect the peso, and also tightened money supply.
Over the weekend, the central bank slashed its M3 or broad money supply to 1,026.8 billion, from 1,056.7 billion.
This means that M3 will only grow by 16.5 percent in 1997, instead of 19.9 percent.
Despite continued currency concerns over the Philippines, the Development Bank of the Philippines launched a yen 20 billion issue of "fixed-rate notes" through Daiwa Securities (HK).
The issue's timing was seen as interesting, given the concerns over the peso, but bankers said the yield might not be enough to relieve bank investors' fears.

While it was good -- it was priced to go at a spread of 110 basis points over yen-yen swaps -- Japanese banks have to make a provision of about 30 percent for Philippine exposure, detracting from the issue's charm.
The only way to avoid this was to keep the debt in the trading account for up to six months.
Japanese branches in other jurisdictions, however, such as Hong Kong, where provisioning is substantially lower, may go for the deal, bankers said.
In other news, Dah Sing Bank Ltd, a unit of Dah Sing Financial Holdings Ltd, is considering issuing the equivalent of US$200 million in floating-rate certificates of deposit.
"We think probably (we will issue) in the second half of the year," a bank executive said.
He said the issue would be either US$200 million, or its equivalent in Hong Kong dollars.
Market talk indicates a five-year issue, but with three- and four-year puts.
The issue will make Dah Sing Bank one of the last to join the flood of issuance in Hong Kong and U.S. dollar FRCDs this year.
If Dah Sing Bank issues in Hong Kong dollars, it will seek eligibility to the liquidity adjustment facility operated by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority.
Dah Sing Bank's last LAF-eligible deal was late in 1996, and was priced at par to float at 40 basis points over the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate for three years.
All-in yield to top-tier lenders was 56 basis but rates have fallen substantially since last year.
Asia Commercial Bank is also tipped to be pondering a Hong Kong dollar FRCD later this year.
In other news, bankers said the HK$3.8 billion syndication for Cheung Kong Infrastructure Finance Co, an arm of Cheung Kong Infrastructure Holdings Ltd, was going slowly.
They said the five-year deal which offers a 48.8 basis point all-in yield was seen as aggressively priced by bankers.
